newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrica Telkom gears for privatisation, competition.
newsitem.headline: SAfrica Telkom gears for privatisation, competition.

text.p: The South African government on Thursday set out rigorous targets aimed at transforming soon-to-be-privatised telecommunications parastatal Telkom from a monopoly into an globally competitive company.

Unveiling a draft of the new Telkom licences at a media briefing, Post and Telecommunications Minister Jay Naidoo said the utility would be given five years of exclusivity during which it had to make telecommunications more accessible, while improving the quality of customer service.

The licences provide Telkom with the right to provide public telecommunications, allow them the use of radio frequencies and the right to provide value-added network services such as electronic mail for the first time in its history.

Among the objectives set out by Naidoo in the draft are the connection of 1.8 million new telephone lines in mainly rural areas and townships, a decrease in the frequency of customer fault reports and reduced tariffs, particularly international call rates which are currently Telkom's main source of revenue.
The achievement of these targets would be monitored by a regulatory authority which would impose fines on Telkom if objectives are not met.

"What is the key is the enormous focus on customer service as we are moving from the situation of a monopoly with no competition and no obligations (to) creating a Telkom that will be customer accountable as its main point of departure," Naidoo said by video link from Cape Town.
"Levels of accountability to customers are substantially increased by the terms of the licence," he said.
Naidoo's announcement comes as the utility moves into the last phase of its partial privatisation, expected to be finalised by April.

SBC Communications Inc and Telekom Malaysia Bhd have said they intend to bid jointly for a 20 to 30 percent stake in Telkom which is expected to net government between five and six billion rand ($1.3 billion), and Deutsche Telekom AG and France Telecom are widely expected to do likewise.
Financial bids for the equity stake were expected to be submitted at the beginning of March, Naidoo said.

He said the process of drawing up the draft licences had undergone vigorous debate with the potential equity partners, which had resulted in a regulatory regime which he felt ranked among the top five in the world.

The three licences, each with a term of 25 years, had drawn heavily on international precedent, particularly those granted to British Telecom in the UK, where the regulatory framework was similar to South Africa's, he said.
They will be submitted for public comment on February 24 and 25 before being issued in April 1997.
